NEW DELHI, India (CNN) — On Wednesday, several hundred Indian soldiers were using boats and helicopters to bring aid to people and evacuate villagers trapped by the most severe floods the region has seen in decades. The disaster followed a breach in an embankment along the Kosi River in Nepal, north of India.

In Bihar, a northeastern Indian state where many affected communities are difficult to access, the number of fatalities remained unclear. K.K. Agarwal, an emergency management official in Bihar, told CNN on Wednesday that 10 people had been confirmed dead. However, the Press Trust of India, or PTI, put the death toll at 55.

Flooded areas were without telephone service and power.

In Birpur, a city in Supaul district, Mohd Rauffudin said his hope was disappearing. Speaking to IBN, CNN’s partner station in India, he said that while struggling to keep himself above water, he became separated from his wife, children, nine brothers and parents.

“I wish the help had reached (us) on time. That way at least my children could have been safe,” he said.

Another survivor, a woman who identified herself as Ruby, told IBN that her baby had been ill for four days, that she had no way to get medical care and that she no longer knew where her family was.

“My child is so ill. I cannot do a thing about it. I wonder what I did wrong that my child must suffer,” she said.

Officials and UNICEF India said the flooding started more than a week earlier, when the Kosi broke through an embankment in Nepal. The waters engulfed villages and destroyed roughly 225,000 homes.

The flow from the rupture was so powerful that the river shifted direction, carving out a new path about 75 miles, or 120 kilometers, east of its usual channel. The diversion sent floodwaters into areas not used to such high water levels.

Agarwal said approximately 2 million people and 725 villages in Bihar, India’s poorest state, had been affected. According to him, authorities had established 95 relief camps, 44 medical camps and 22 shelters for livestock.

Lt. Col. A.K. Mathur, an army spokesman, said 400 soldiers were taking part in rescue efforts and that the military had sent at least 20 rescue boats. He also said three army helicopters were dropping thousands of food packets.

Earlier Wednesday, PTI reported that poor weather had stopped Indian air force helicopters from making relief drops in Bihar’s worst-affected districts: Supaul, Saharsa, Araria and Madhepura.

Officials told CNN the flooding was the worst Bihar had experienced in 80 years.

The Kosi River is often called the “River of Sorrow” in India because it floods during the monsoon season, which runs from June through September. The river eventually joins the Ganges, a river considered sacred by Hindus.

Video footage showed people gathered on the roofs of low buildings, standing in streets filled with waist-deep water and attempting to flee by boat. Floodwaters had covered roads and railway lines and knocked out electricity.

# Kosi River Breach Triggers Devastating Floods in Bihar as Rescue Teams Race to Reach Stranded Villages

**PATNA, India** — A massive breach in an embankment on the Kosi River in neighboring Nepal has unleashed devastating floods across parts of India’s eastern Bihar state, submerging villages, sweeping away homes and leaving hundreds of thousands of people scrambling for safety.

Authorities said the river broke through an embankment near the Nepal-India border, forcing the Kosi — often called Bihar’s “Sorrow” because of its long history of destructive floods — to surge into areas that had not seen its main flow in decades. The sudden shift sent torrents of water across low-lying districts, including Supaul, Madhepura, Araria, Saharsa and Purnia.

The full death toll remains unclear. Officials have confirmed casualties, but they warned that the number could rise sharply as rescue teams reach cut-off villages and floodwaters recede. Many communities remain inaccessible, with roads washed out, power lines down and communication networks disrupted.

“We ran with only the clothes we were wearing,” said Meena Devi, a resident of a flooded village in Supaul district, describing the panic as water rushed through her neighborhood. “There was no time to save anything. The water came like a wall.”

Another survivor, Mohammad Salim, said his family spent the night on the roof of their home before being rescued by boat. “We shouted for help for hours,” he said. “Children were crying, and the elderly could not move. We thought no one would find us.”

## Rescue Operations Underway

Indian authorities have deployed disaster response teams, police, army personnel and local volunteers to evacuate stranded residents. Rescue boats are moving through submerged villages, while helicopters have been used in some areas to drop food packets and identify people trapped on rooftops and raised patches of land.

Officials said priority is being given to children, pregnant women, the elderly and those requiring medical attention. Thousands of people have been moved to relief camps set up in schools, government buildings and temporary shelters on higher ground.

“The situation is extremely serious,” a state disaster management official said. “Water has spread across a vast area, and many villages are still difficult to reach. Our immediate focus is rescue, food, clean drinking water and medical support.”

Local residents say the scale of the disaster has overwhelmed many communities. In several places, families have tied livestock to trees or abandoned animals altogether as they fled rising water. Others are waiting on embankments and roads, hoping for transport to relief centers.

## Relief Camps Face Growing Pressure

Relief operations are expanding, but officials and aid groups warn that the needs are enormous. Camps are facing shortages of clean water, sanitation facilities, baby food and medicines. Doctors have raised concerns about waterborne diseases, including diarrhea, skin infections and fever, as displaced families crowd into temporary shelters.

“We have food for now, but there are too many people coming every hour,” said one relief volunteer working near Madhepura. “Many have not eaten properly for days.”

Government agencies said they are distributing rice, lentils, dry food, tarpaulins, candles and chlorine tablets. Medical teams have been sent to relief centers, and vaccination drives are being planned to prevent disease outbreaks.

The breach has also raised questions about embankment maintenance and cross-border flood management between India and Nepal. Experts have long warned that silt buildup and pressure on aging embankments make the Kosi especially dangerous during heavy monsoon rains.

For survivors, the concern is more immediate: finding loved ones, securing food and deciding when — or whether — they can return home.

“I don’t know if my house is still there,” said Devi. “I don’t know where we will go after this. We have lost everything.”

Officials said rescue operations will continue around the clock as long as weather and water conditions allow. But with large areas still underwater and more rain possible, authorities warned that Bihar’s flood emergency is far from over.

**Kosi River breach unleashes humanitarian crisis in northeastern India**

**PATNA, India —** A massive breach in the embankments of the Kosi River triggered one of India’s worst flood disasters in years, forcing hundreds of thousands of people from their homes across northeastern Bihar and leaving large swaths of farmland, villages and roads submerged, officials and aid agencies said.

The disaster began after the Kosi, a Himalayan river notorious for shifting course, burst through an embankment near Kusaha in neighboring Nepal in mid-August 2008. The river then abandoned much of its existing channel and surged eastward into an old course it had not occupied for decades, sending torrents of water across densely populated districts of Bihar.

Indian officials said the sudden change in the river’s path devastated districts including Supaul, Madhepura, Araria, Saharsa and Purnea. Villages were cut off, homes collapsed, crops were destroyed and thousands of families took shelter on highways, embankments, school buildings and any raised ground they could reach.

The Press Trust of India reported that rescue teams, including personnel from the army, air force, National Disaster Response Force and state agencies, were deployed to evacuate stranded residents by boat and helicopter. Relief operations were hampered by washed-out roads, strong currents and the sheer scale of the inundation.

Bihar officials described the situation as a major humanitarian emergency. The state government said hundreds of relief camps were opened and food, drinking water, tarpaulins and medical teams were being sent to affected areas. Authorities also expressed concern over outbreaks of waterborne disease as floodwaters contaminated wells and other drinking-water sources.

UNICEF said children were among the most vulnerable survivors, with many separated from their homes, exposed to unsafe water and at risk of illness in crowded relief camps. The agency supported emergency supplies including water-purification materials, hygiene kits, medicines and nutritional assistance, and worked with state authorities to help restore basic services.

Aid workers reported urgent needs for clean water, sanitation, shelter and medical care. In many camps, families who had escaped with little more than the clothes they were wearing waited for food distribution and news of relatives left behind.

Eyewitnesses described a flood that arrived with little warning.

Residents of Supaul and Madhepura districts said water rushed through villages in the middle of the night or early morning, sweeping away livestock, grain stores and household belongings. Some said they climbed onto rooftops or trees before being rescued. Others waded for hours through chest-deep water carrying children or elderly relatives.

“We heard people shouting that the river had come,” one displaced resident from a submerged village told reporters. “By the time we understood what was happening, the water was already inside the house. We left everything behind.”

Another survivor sheltering along a raised road said families had no time to save food or documents. “The fields are gone, the animals are gone. We do not know when we can return,” he said.

The Kosi, sometimes called the “Sorrow of Bihar,” has a long history of destructive floods because of heavy silt loads from the Himalayas and its tendency to shift course across the plains. Embankments built to contain the river have reduced routine flooding in some areas but have also created risks when they fail, experts say.

The 2008 breach was especially destructive because it occurred upstream in Nepal, allowing the river to carve a new path into areas that had not seen such flows for generations. Many settlements in the newly flooded zone were not prepared for a major river channel to run through them.

Indian and Nepalese authorities faced questions over embankment maintenance and cross-border flood management. Officials said the immediate priority was rescue and relief, but engineers and disaster-management specialists warned that repairing the breach and guiding the river back to its previous channel would be an enormous challenge.

As floodwaters spread, the central government announced assistance for Bihar, while political leaders visited affected districts and promised compensation for families who lost relatives, homes or crops. Relief agencies cautioned that recovery would take months, with thousands of families likely to remain displaced long after the water receded.

For survivors, the disaster left uncertainty as profound as the damage.

“Our village is under the river now,” one resident said. “We do not know if there will be anything to go back to.”

# Catastrophic Monsoon Flooding Swamps Bihar After Nepal Embankment Breach

**By Staff Reporter**  
**Patna/Supaul, Bihar —** Torrential monsoon rains and a reported embankment breach upstream in Nepal have unleashed devastating floods across parts of northern Bihar, submerging villages, cutting off roads and forcing thousands of families to flee to rooftops, highways and makeshift relief camps.

Officials said the sudden surge of water entered low-lying areas after a protective embankment along the Kosi river system was damaged in Nepal, sending floodwaters rushing into districts including Supaul, Saharsa, Araria, Madhepura and Purnea. Local authorities described the situation as “critical,” with rescue teams racing against time to reach stranded residents.

## “The Water Came Like a Wall”

In Supaul district, entire hamlets were under water by early morning, with only treetops, electricity poles and the upper floors of homes visible above the muddy current.

“The water came like a wall,” said **Meena Devi**, a resident of a village near the Kosi’s floodplain, speaking from a relief boat with her two children. “We heard people shouting in the night. By the time we stepped outside, the courtyard was gone. We climbed onto the roof and waited for help.”

Another survivor, **Mohammad Irfan**, said his family had lost livestock, stored grain and important documents. “We have nothing left except the clothes we are wearing,” he said. “The river took our home in minutes.”

Villagers said the speed of the flooding left little time for evacuation. Many families reported spending hours in the rain before being rescued by boats operated by the National Disaster Response Force and local volunteers.

## Military and Disaster Teams Deployed

The Indian Army, Air Force and National Disaster Response Force have been deployed to assist with rescue and relief operations. Officials said military helicopters were being used to conduct aerial surveys and drop food packets, drinking water, tarpaulins and medical supplies in areas inaccessible by road.

Army engineering units were also helping reinforce vulnerable embankments and restore temporary access routes, while inflatable boats and motorized rescue craft ferried stranded residents to safer ground.

A senior disaster management official said priority was being given to the elderly, pregnant women, children and people requiring medical care. “The main challenge is the force of the current and the number of villages cut off,” the official said. “We are expanding rescue operations as water levels and weather conditions allow.”

Relief camps have been opened in schools, panchayat buildings and elevated areas. Medical teams are monitoring for waterborne diseases, snakebites and infections, which often rise after major floods.

## Roads Washed Out, Power Disrupted

Several rural roads and small bridges have reportedly been damaged or washed away, complicating relief efforts. Power supply has been disrupted in many inundated areas as a precaution, while mobile networks remain patchy.

Residents in affected districts said food and clean drinking water were becoming urgent concerns.

“We have been here since yesterday,” said **Ramesh Yadav**, sheltering with dozens of others on a raised embankment. “Children are hungry. We need milk, medicine and dry food. The boats come, but there are too many people waiting.”

Officials have appealed to people not to return to flooded homes until water levels recede and structures are inspected for safety.

## The Kosi: Bihar’s “River of Sorrow”

The Kosi river, often called the **“River of Sorrow”**, has a long history of destructive flooding in Bihar. Flowing from the Himalayas through Nepal into India, the river carries massive volumes of silt and frequently shifts course across the plains.

For generations, the Kosi’s changing channels have devastated farmland and settlements. Embankments were built to contain the river, but experts have repeatedly warned that heavy siltation, extreme rainfall and pressure on flood-control structures can increase the risk of breaches.

The most infamous recent disaster occurred in 2008, when a breach in the Kosi embankment in Nepal caused the river to change course, flooding large parts of Bihar and displacing millions. The latest flooding has revived fears among residents who remember that catastrophe.

“My father used to say the Kosi never forgets its old path,” said **Sita Kumari**, a teacher from Saharsa district. “Every monsoon we live with fear. This time, the fear became real again.”

## Authorities Urge Vigilance

Bihar’s disaster management department has asked residents in vulnerable areas to move to higher ground and follow evacuation advisories. Control rooms have been activated, and officials said coordination is underway with authorities in Nepal to monitor river levels and embankment conditions.

Weather forecasters have warned that more rainfall is possible in the catchment areas over the coming days, raising concerns that flood levels could remain dangerous.

For thousands of families across northern Bihar, the immediate focus remains survival.

“We don’t know when we can go back,” Meena Devi said, holding her son close as rescue workers guided families toward a relief camp. “If our house is still there, we will rebuild. But first, we need to live.”
